text: Kitty about one month old. Has lived outdoors in the desert all it's life. All this time has only interacted with one living being - me.

My kitty is growing. About a month old now. Not sure about feeding schedule. I just feel her  tummy to see how full it is. She always wants something from me. Must sleep in my tent under my chin. Nights get into the 40s.  She loves to sit or play in the morning sun. Days are in the 80s now. Time to arrive here is no sooner than late October. 

Hot baths are not good for abdominal wall. Hernia becomes troublesome. I guess cold weather may be best for me. Learn Learn something new everyday. The hot baths help in other ways, but cold is likely best.

Just as moving into a new home or apartment can take months to become settled and comfortable, so too with establishing a long term campsite. You slowly come to realize the hazards, threats, annoyances and opportunities. 

Here are a few detailed photos of my hotspring campsite in Imperial County, California.  This camp is 5 miles from the US Mexico border, and actively patrolled by US Border Patrol agents. All too often there are helicopters overhead, and sometimes late at night I can hear the choppers to the south working the border. 

Once an off-road border patrol vehicle passed 20 feet from my camp, and then proceeded to back out, passing my camp again as he was unable to proceed forward. The agent did not spot my camp.

Over time, tools and furnishings are found and acquired. Although I rarely build a fire, cooking equipment and firewood are readily available, and I have a large ice chest buried underground. 

All items are found as discards from the main camping area dumping grounds where the more well-to-do folks with the Recreational Vehicles congregate. Even the cast iron cookware was found discarded. 

The food supply is all freely acquired as well, both in the town 8 mile away, and on the "free table" located at the main RV parking area. Even good fresh coffee is found discarded.

Kitty has her own sleeping and eating area, but with most winter nights in the low 40s F, she insists on sleeping with me in my tent. She is not yet fully trained, so I need to be attentive to let her out every few hours.

There are wild predator animals just outside my camp. I am not sure what sort of animals they are, but at night I hear them snarling as they go after and kill their prey.

Since kitty was about a week old, I would put her 6 feet (2m) up on a tree limb, and she slowly learned how to climb down. Now at about 5 weeks old, she can climb the same tree on her own, even higher, and up different branch systems.

I am surprised to see her climb that tree 5 or 6 times each day now. Surely she is developing the ability to escape any wild predator that may enter our camp. But for the most part, predators will avoid humans and their camps when occupied for the long term.

I would say she's about 3 to 4 times the size and weight compared to when I found first her, apparently only a couple days old. 

Autumn nights are now in the low 40s F, and she especially enjoys playing in the morning sun as the days heat up to the mid 90s F.

As yet, she has never left camp, never interacted with another human or animal, but she does pay some attention to ants.  I am not certain if she is aware of the birds or geckos, but does notice various sounds.
I am beginning to think she is a stray wild bobcat cub.

Always enjoy daytime hardcopy reading, conserves battery power.

Not certain why I have not been approached. I check for tracking twice a day. The choppers fly overhead everyday,  sometimes the Ospreys. 

Could it be I am so well hidden? Logistically, I could explain to you a dozen factors why the odds are in my favor.

Why do you think everyone is leaving me alone? I have not detected a human here for over two years.

Transporting a kitten on a bicycle can be done with a bit of preparation. Consider using a secure and well-ventilated pet carrier or a small, sturdy box with air holes. Place soft bedding inside for comfort.

Attach the carrier or box securely to the bicycle using bungee cords or straps. Ensure it's stable and won't shift during the ride. Keep the carrier in a position where you can easily monitor your kitten while cycling.

Start with short rides to let her acclimate to the experience. Always prioritize her safety and well-being during transportation.

Mattias Desmet is a Belgian clinical psychologist and professor known for his work on the psychological aspects of totalitarianism. He argues that mass formation, a psychological state characterized by a collective feeling of discontent, can contribute to the rise of totalitarian movements. Desmet suggests that factors like social isolation and a sense of powerlessness play a role in shaping this psychological state.
